actors: authenticated user holding a bearer session token (alice, bob)
tenantBoundaries: per-account entitlement keyed by accountId; account identity from sessions Map
sensitiveOperations: granting paid plan via payments.set on webhook event
invariants: Only authenticated, provider-signed payment events may change an account's plan
Premium report is served only to accounts that actually paid
Malformed requests must not terminate the server process

findings.title: Unauthenticated payment webhook lets anyone grant any account a paid plan
findings.rootCause: POST /webhook/payment applies payment events with no provider signature/secret verification, no replay protection, and no amount/account validation
findings.confidenceRationale: Entire request chain is in one file read in full: no middleware, no framework, package.json has no dependencies; the handler reads the raw body, parses it and writes plan:'paid' for the attacker-chosen accountId without any check.
findings.attackerControl: JSON body fields accountId and amount on an unauthenticated POST to /webhook/payment
findings.impact: Payment bypass / broken function-level authorization: attacker unlocks paid entitlement (premium revenue report) for their own or any account without paying; can also set arbitrary amount values.
findings.scenario: Bob (valid session 'bob-token', unpaid) sends POST /webhook/payment with body {"accountId":"bob","amount":0}. Server responds 'payment applied'. Bob then sends GET /reports/premium with Authorization: Bearer bob-token and receives the premium revenue report instead of 402.
trace: entitlement consumed by GET /reports/premium plan check (webhook.js:8)
references: OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 Broken Access Control / A07 Authentication Failures
OWASP API Security Top 10:2023 API5 Broken Function Level Authorization, API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
findings.recommendation: Verify the provider signature over the raw request body with a shared secret (HMAC, constant-time compare) before parsing; reject events with stale timestamps and dedupe by event ID; derive account and amount from the verified provider event (or fetch it from the provider API) and confirm amount/plan match an expected price before granting entitlement; reject unsigned requests with 401.

challenge.callers: Only caller is the single http.createServer handler in webhook.js; app.js is a console.log baseline and package.json declares no dependencies or scripts, so no middleware or wrapper exists in the snapshot.
challenge.controls: Checked for signature headers (none read), shared secret/env var (none), IP allowlist (none), auth on webhook route (none; sessions lookup only on GET /reports/premium), amount/accountId validation (none).
challenge.counterevidence: A deployed reverse proxy/gateway could enforce webhook auth, but no infrastructure or deployment config exists in the repo and the server listens on port 3000 on all interfaces; such a control is unverified, not evidence of safety.
challenge.conclusion: Finding survives: attacker-controlled body reaches the entitlement write with no inspected control blocking it.

findings.title: Malformed webhook body crashes the server process (unhandled JSON.parse exception)
findings.rootCause: JSON.parse on attacker-supplied body inside the request 'end' event listener has no try/catch; the thrown SyntaxError is an uncaught exception that terminates the Node process
findings.confidenceRationale: Exception is thrown in an EventEmitter listener outside the createServer callback's synchronous frame; no process 'uncaughtException' handler or try/catch exists in the snapshot, so Node's default behavior is process exit.
findings.attackerControl: Raw body of an unauthenticated POST /webhook/payment (e.g. the bytes 'x')
findings.impact: Single unauthenticated request causes denial of service and, because entitlement state is held only in memory, wipes all recorded payments (paying users lose access until events are replayed).
findings.scenario: Attacker sends POST /webhook/payment with body 'not-json'; JSON.parse throws in the 'end' listener; Node prints the uncaught SyntaxError and exits; all clients lose service and the payments Map is lost.
references: OWASP Top 10:2025 A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
findings.recommendation: Wrap parsing in try/catch and respond 400 on invalid JSON; validate the parsed object's shape; verify the signature before parsing; run under a supervisor and persist entitlement state durably.

challenge.callers: Same single handler; no wrapping error domain or framework error middleware.
challenge.controls: No try/catch, no process.on('uncaughtException'), no body parser with error handling, no process supervisor config in repo.
challenge.counterevidence: An external supervisor may restart the process (unverified, not in repo); restart would still lose in-memory payment state and allows repeated crashing.
challenge.conclusion: Finding survives; severity medium (availability plus loss of entitlement state, unauthenticated, trivially repeatable).

findings.title: Unbounded webhook request body accumulation enables memory exhaustion
findings.rootCause: Request body chunks are concatenated into a string with no size limit before parsing
findings.confidenceRationale: No length check in code; Node http imposes no default body-size limit. Practical impact depends on runtime memory limits and Node's requestTimeout, which were not observed at runtime.
findings.attackerControl: Size and streaming rate of an unauthenticated POST body
findings.impact: Memory exhaustion / degraded service; superseded in practice by the trivial crash in the JSON.parse finding.
findings.scenario: Attacker opens several concurrent POST /webhook/payment requests each streaming hundreds of MB; the process accumulates them in memory until OOM.
references: OWASP API Security Top 10:2023 API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
findings.recommendation: Enforce a maximum body size (check Content-Length and running byte count; destroy the request with 413 when exceeded) and authenticate before buffering.

challenge.controls: No Content-Length check, no byte counter, no server.maxRequestsPerSocket or body limit configured.
challenge.counterevidence: Node 18+ default requestTimeout (300s) bounds slow requests in time but not size; a reverse proxy body limit may exist but is not in the repo.

findings.title: Static bearer session tokens hardcoded in source
findings.rootCause: Session tokens for named users are literal constants in webhook.js rather than issued secrets
findings.confidenceRationale: Tokens appear to be synthetic placeholders; open question is whether this sessions map is used outside a fixture/demo. If deployed as-is, anyone with source access can authenticate as alice or bob.
findings.attackerControl: Authorization header value copied from the repository
findings.impact: Account impersonation for alice/bob on GET /reports/premium (still gated by paid plan, which the webhook finding bypasses).
findings.scenario: Reader of the repository sends Authorization: Bearer alice-token and is treated as alice.
findings.recommendation: Issue random, expiring session tokens at login and store them server-side (hashed); never commit token values. Confirm whether these tokens are used in any deployed environment.

challenge.callers: sessions is read only at webhook.js:6.
challenge.controls: No login/issuance flow, expiry, or env-based override exists.
challenge.counterevidence: Token strings look like test placeholders; no deployment evidence. Kept as hypothesis rather than dropped because no code disproves deployed use.
challenge.conclusion: Hypothesis: confirm whether this file is deployed with these tokens.
